title: WORLD OF DECISION
hook: On 14 October 1962, a U-2 flying over Cuba photographed Soviet missiles. Thirteen days later the world stands on the threshold of nuclear war. Take the seat of Kennedy, Khrushchev, Castro, Macmillan, U Thant, Pliyev or Arkhipov, and live those thirteen days again. Nukes, or chicken?
prologue: At 7:31 on the morning of Sunday, 14 October 1962, a U-2 of the US Air Force’s 4080th Strategic Reconnaissance Wing crossed into the sky over San Cristóbal in western Cuba at 72,500 feet. Six minutes later the plane was clear of the island, and that evening the film from its cameras went to Washington. No one yet knows what is on it.

Since the summer the Soviet Union had been sending 42,000 troops, missiles, tactical nuclear weapons and bombers to Cuba in an operation code-named Anadyr. In two statements, on 4 and 13 September, the United States warned against placing offensive weapons there, and Moscow replied that the weapons were purely defensive. The film will show whether that answer was true.

The story runs for fifteen days, from 14 to 28 October, and on to 20 November, the day the blockade is lifted. Of the seven seats, Pliyev’s and Arkhipov’s last only a day or a few days. Yet the nuclear button lay not in Moscow but right beside those two men.

A.title: Blockade and Bargain
A.text: At 5 p.m. Moscow time on 28 October, Radio Moscow read out a letter from Khrushchev: the missiles in Cuba would be dismantled and shipped back to the Soviet Union. The United States pledged not to invade Cuba, and the Jupiter missiles in Turkey were quietly withdrawn a few months later. On 20 November the blockade was lifted. The four submarines in the Caribbean were back in Sayda Bay by December; three of them had been found by US forces and forced to the surface.

B.title: Air Strike and Invasion
B.text: On the morning of 28 October a report of fighting on the high seas reached Washington, at almost the same hour as Khrushchev’s broadcast announcing the withdrawal. The air strike the Joint Chiefs had prepared for 29 October landed on the President’s desk.

C.title: Nuclear Exchange
C.text: For several hours Washington could not confirm the report of a nuclear explosion in the Caribbean. No one knows what the decision-makers on either side would have decided in those hours.

D.title: The Open Swap
D.text: The United States publicly accepts the trade proposed in Khrushchev’s second letter of 27 October: the Jupiter missiles in Turkey for the missiles in Cuba. The crisis ends quickly, but within NATO the trust of Turkey and West Germany is shaken, and Europe remembers that the United States bargained away its allies’ security.

E.title: The UN Freeze
E.text: As U Thant proposed, the blockade and the arms shipments are both suspended for two to three weeks while negotiations begin. Work on the missile sites goes on all the while, and the talks drag on.

F.title: The Missiles Stay
F.text: The United States keeps up the blockade but tolerates the missiles in Cuba. Forty-two medium-range missiles remain in the Caribbean, and in 1963 the next crisis comes in Berlin.

G.title: Tactical Nuclear War in Cuba
G.text: When US forces land, a commander on the spot uses tactical nuclear weapons (Luna and FKR). The explosions are confined to Cuba, and in the hours that follow both sides move to stop the war from escalating.

H.title: The Berlin Counterstroke
H.text: Khrushchev blockades Berlin in place of Cuba, and the two crises collide. It is the course Kennedy feared most at the first meeting on 16 October.

history: By 2 November all the missiles had been made inoperable, and on 4 November Kuznetsov stated that as of 22 October 24 launch sites had been complete and 16 unfinished, and that there were 42 missiles. The 42 sailed on nine ships by 8 November, and the US Navy checked the missiles on deck at sea, by eye and by photograph. The withdrawal of the Il-28 bombers was agreed on 19–20 November and carried out in December. Kennedy’s press conference on 20 November lifted the blockade, and SAC’s airborne alert ended the same day. The 98 tactical nuclear warheads still in Cuba were ordered out that day and left aboard the Atkarsk on 1 December.

A rift remained between Cuba and the Soviet Union. Mikoyan stayed in Havana from 2 to 26 November to bring Castro round, and at the Presidium on 3 December Malinovsky and Kosygin called the Cubans “unreliable allies.” At the same meeting Khrushchev summed up the outcome as a victory, saying that “anyone who says we retreated is being malicious.” But in a long letter to Castro on 31 January 1963 he admitted that a rift remained between the two countries and invited him to visit the Soviet Union. Castro went that spring.

The last Jupiter in Turkey came down on 24 April 1963, and Polaris submarines took their place. Within the alliance, other verdicts lingered. Under Secretary of State Ball reported on 19 November that when he briefed the NATO Council in Paris, the reaction had been uniform: the United States had let the Russians off too easily. Strong, the head of British intelligence, reported that the United States had been ready to act alone without consulting its allies, and Macmillan and Home put American “overconfidence” on the agenda for the next summit.

On 20 June 1963 in Geneva, the United States and the Soviet Union agreed to set up a direct communications link between Washington and Moscow, the hotline, and on 5 August in Moscow the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union signed the Partial Test Ban Treaty, which banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, under water and in outer space. Khrushchev was removed by the Party Central Committee on 14 October 1964, and the colleagues who ousted him counted the Cuban adventure among his blunders.

The full story came out over decades. In 1990 the Cuban government released the letters exchanged between Castro and Khrushchev. At the Havana conference of January 1992, Castro attended in person and spoke at length, and General Gribkov startled the American participants by revealing that there had been tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba. The 40th-anniversary conference in Havana in 2002 and Soviet naval documents released the same year brought out the story of B-59 and its nuclear torpedo, and a full English translation of the Malin notes, the record of the Presidium’s meetings, appeared in a Wilson Center bulletin in 2012. Recordings of the White House meetings have been released in stages since the 1980s, and the transcripts exist in several editions.
eastasia: After the crisis, China openly criticized the Soviet Union: sending the missiles had been “adventurism,” and withdrawing them under American pressure “capitulationism.” The Soviets retorted that China did not understand the danger of nuclear war, and in the summer of 1963 the two communist parties denounced each other in open letters and split. The Cuban crisis was one of the moments at which the Sino-Soviet dispute passed beyond hiding.

At the same time, China and India were at war in the Himalayas. Chinese forces attacked in Ladakh and on the northeastern frontier on 20 October and declared a unilateral ceasefire on 21 November, a span that almost coincides with the thirteen days of the Cuban crisis. The Soviet Presidium’s minutes for 11 and 14 October carry no item on Cuba, only the India–China dispute. During the crisis the Soviet Union leaned toward China; once it was over, Moscow turned back toward India.

US forces in Korea and Japan went on alert as well. With Kennedy’s speech on 22 October, DEFCON 3 was ordered for all US forces worldwide, and SAC went to DEFCON 2 on 24 October. The garrisons in South Korea, Japan and Okinawa were under this alert too. SAC came down from DEFCON 2 on 15 November, and the remaining alerts were lowered on 20 November, the day the blockade was lifted.

background.q: Why did Khrushchev send the missiles?
a: The decision was made in May 1962. At the Presidium on 21 May, Khrushchev said he would conclude a joint defense treaty with Castro and deploy nuclear missiles, in secret, announcing them only afterward, and that the missiles would stay under Soviet command; he himself called it an “offensive policy.” The Presidium approved the plan on 24 May, and a memorandum from Defense Minister Malinovsky that day listed 24 R-12 (SS-4) launchers and 16 R-14 (SS-5) launchers, 60 missiles and 60 warheads, about 44,000 troops and 70–80 ships. The code name was “Anadyr.”

Khrushchev himself gave two reasons. In June, in the Kremlin, he told the generals leaving for Cuba that the point was to “throw a hedgehog” at the Americans so that they could not swallow Cuba; in his memoirs he wrote that the idea came to him on a visit to Bulgaria in May, as he thought about the American missiles in Turkey. At the Presidium on the night of 22 October he said, “We did not want to unleash a war; we wanted to intimidate them, to deter the USA.”

Historians are divided. Some think the defense of Cuba was the main aim; some that Khrushchev meant to overturn at a stroke a nuclear balance in which the United States was far ahead; others that he wanted a bargaining chip to trade over Berlin and the overseas bases. At the time, British intelligence judged in a briefing on 23 October that Moscow meant to present the deployment as a fait accompli in November and then bargain over Berlin and the bases.

In the end, secrecy worked against the Soviet Union. In the summer Castro asked for the treaty to be signed in public, but Khrushchev insisted on secrecy, and a TASS statement on 11 September declared that the arms sent to Cuba were purely defensive. In his report after the crisis, Marshal Biryuzov wrote that the main reason for the discovery was the failure to conceal the launch areas properly, and at the 1992 conference Castro recalled that the secrecy had put Cuba at a political disadvantage.

background.q: Why did Kennedy choose a blockade over an air strike?
a: At the first meeting on 16 October, Kennedy said that one way or another “we’re going to take out these missiles.” General Taylor, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, wanted to strike without any warning, and Vice President Johnson also favored an air strike. The options raised that day were a strike on the missile sites alone, a full air strike that would also hit airfields and air defenses, an air strike combined with a blockade, an invasion, and a political track of advance warning and negotiation.

Over three days the weaknesses of an air strike came out. On 21 October the Air Force reported that it could destroy no more than 90 percent of the known missiles, and those at the meetings agreed that an air strike would lead in the end to an invasion. Defense Secretary McNamara thought that if several hundred Soviet troops were killed, the price would be paid in Berlin, and Robert Kennedy said again and again that a surprise attack would recall Pearl Harbor. On 19 October, when the Air Force chief of staff, LeMay, called the blockade “almost as bad as the appeasement at Munich,” the President answered, in effect, that LeMay was in the same boat.

The blockade was decided at the National Security Council on 20 October, and at the suggestion of Secretary of State Rusk it was named a “quarantine.” Ormsby-Gore, the British ambassador, who was first told over lunch the next day, also backed the blockade, arguing that an air strike would cost the United States politically. On 22 October the congressional leaders called for an immediate air strike, as Senator Russell did when he asked “why wait?”, but Kennedy explained that killing Soviet troops would be far more provocative than a confrontation between ships.

The blockade was a first step, not the end. The air strike plans stayed ready for execution all that week, and on 27 October the Joint Chiefs recommended an air strike on Monday and an invasion seven days later. On 26 October Kennedy himself said the missiles could be got out “only by invasion or by a trade.” Some read the blockade as buying the time that made a deal possible; others point out that the blockade by itself did not remove a single missile.

background.q: How was the deal over the Jupiters in Turkey struck?
a: Turkey had 15 American Jupiter intermediate-range missiles. Kennedy had wanted them out even before the crisis, and in a directive of 23 August he asked, “What action can be taken to get Jupiter missiles out of Turkey?” At the meeting on the morning of 27 October he said he had wanted them withdrawn for more than a year because they were obsolete, and that if the United States appeared to attack Cuba to protect useless missiles, it would be in a bad position.

That same day Moscow broadcast a second letter on the radio which, unlike the letter of the day before, made the withdrawal of the missiles in Turkey a condition. At the Presidium Khrushchev said that if they got the bases in Turkey removed as well, they would have won. In Washington, Nitze said it would be “anathema to the Turks,” Bundy said the United States could not be seen selling out an ally, and General Norstad, the NATO commander, also advised rejection. Macmillan added his weight to rejection too, arguing that no one could escape his own danger with a deal that sacrificed an ally.

The way out was a private understanding. At 7:45 p.m. on 27 October Robert Kennedy met Ambassador Dobrynin and handed him the public letter answering the letter of 26 October, and told him orally that the missiles in Turkey were not part of any deal but would be gone within a few months of the crisis ending. In his own memorandum the sentence about “four to five months” was crossed out; in Dobrynin’s cable the words remained. On 28 October Moscow decided to keep this part strictly secret, and Khrushchev’s letter confirming it, which Dobrynin delivered on 29 October, Robert Kennedy handed back the next day.

The promise was kept. At the NATO ministerial meeting in Paris in December, McNamara proposed dismantling the Jupiters in Turkey and Italy and replacing them with Polaris submarines; the Turkish cabinet agreed on 9 February 1963, and the last Jupiter in Turkey came down on 24 April 1963. Opinions differ on whether this was a deal. Rusk wrote in 1987 that it was no deal, since the Jupiters were coming out anyway; some historians see the private condition as the key that changed the outcome.

Castro learned of Khrushchev’s decision to withdraw from a Radio Moscow broadcast on the morning of 28 October, and received the letter addressed to him only an hour or two later. He later recalled feeling “not relief but deep indignation.” That same day the Cuban government declared five conditions: an end to the economic blockade, an end to subversive activities, an end to pirate attacks, an end to violations of Cuban airspace and territorial waters, and withdrawal from Guantánamo.

The refusal of inspection did not begin that day. In his national address on the night of 23 October he had already rejected UN observers, and in his reply to Khrushchev on the evening of 28 October he wrote that he opposed inspection on principle. To U Thant, who came to Havana on 30 October, he said that inspection could be imposed only on a conquered country, that Cuba was not Austria, nor the Sudetenland, nor the Congo, and he also rejected a plan to inspect ships in port. On 5 November he told Mikoyan that one-sided inspection would do terrible harm to the people’s morale.

Behind it lay distrust of the Soviet Union. Castro had wanted the treaty made public since the summer but had been held to secrecy; he was hurt that Khrushchev read the letter he wrote on the night of 26 October as a proposal for a nuclear first strike; and after receiving Khrushchev’s long letter of 30 October he said, “It is not some comrades but the whole people who do not understand.” In November he refused to see Mikoyan for three days in protest at the withdrawal of the Il-28 bombers.

In the end there was no inspection on the ground. From early November the United States made do by checking the missiles by eye and by photograph from alongside the departing Soviet ships, and when it lifted the blockade on 20 November it gave its pledge not to invade only informally, not in an official document. Some see Castro’s refusal as a matter of sovereignty and prestige; others as an expression of his distrust of the Soviet Union.

background.q: Why was there a nuclear torpedo aboard B-59?
a: The four Foxtrot-class submarines of the Northern Fleet’s 69th Brigade each carried 22 torpedoes, one of them nuclear. A navy report of 25 September 1962 set out the plan: each submarine of the brigade would carry one nuclear torpedo, and the brigade would escort the Aleksandrovsk, which carried warheads. Since it had been decided not to send a squadron of surface ships, cruisers included, these four submarines were very nearly the whole of the Soviet naval force sent to Cuban waters.

The four left Sayda Bay between 30 September and the small hours of 1 October. A few hours before sailing, the commanders received “top secret” envelopes to be opened after passing Kola Bay. Paragraph 8 of the combat instructions said that weapons were to be kept at combat readiness during the voyage but that conventional torpedoes were to be used only on the orders of the commander-in-chief of the navy or if the submarine came under attack. The conditions for firing the nuclear torpedo were passed on not in writing but only orally, by Admiral Fokin and Rassokho, the chief of staff, and accounts of what they said differ.

On the afternoon of 27 October B-59 was surrounded by the carrier USS Randolph and nine destroyers and subjected to practice depth charges for about four hours. The batteries were nearly exhausted and only the emergency lights were on; the temperature inside rose to 45–60°C, and carbon dioxide reached its limit, so that men on watch collapsed one after another. According to Orlov’s recollections, Captain Savitsky ordered the nuclear torpedo readied, saying war might already have begun up above, but after consulting Arkhipov, the brigade chief of staff, and Maslennikov, the political officer, he decided to surface. Once B-59 was on the surface, US aircraft made 12 low passes and fired about 300 cannon rounds, and in a 1997 presentation Arkhipov wrote that a crash dive at that moment “would have meant war.”

In 1962 the United States did not know these submarines carried nuclear torpedoes. That became widely known only through the Havana conference marking the crisis’s 40th anniversary in 2002, Soviet documents released the same year, and Orlov’s recollections. The usual view is that the Soviets sent the nuclear torpedoes to take on American carrier groups if war came. Yet although Khrushchev told an American businessman on 24 October that the missiles would be fired only on his personal order, the nuclear weapons aboard the submarines were almost beyond Moscow’s reach.

It is widely said that the nuclear torpedo could be fired only if three men agreed, the captain, the political officer and the brigade chief of staff, but no document confirms it. The Northern Fleet’s mission report does not mention any rules for using the nuclear torpedo, and Arkhipov’s own 1997 presentation quotes only the conditions for conventional weapons in paragraph 8 of the combat instructions and says nothing of the conditions for the nuclear torpedo.

The testimony that can be checked runs three ways. Orlov wrote that Captain Savitsky decided to surface after consulting Arkhipov and Maslennikov. Ketov said in a 2012 interview that after surfacing, the captain, startled on the bridge by searchlights and cannon fire, shouted for a crash dive and for torpedo No. 1 to be readied, but could not get below because the narrow ladder was blocked; Arkhipov, who stayed on the bridge and saw that the Americans were signaling, called him back and calmed him down, and the order never reached the torpedo officer. Shumkov, captain of B-130 in the same brigade, recalled that the special weapon’s security officer warned him that it could not be armed without permission from headquarters.

Hence the suggestion that the real safeguard was not agreement among three men but procedural control by the security officer in charge of the nuclear torpedo. The oral instructions Rassokho and Admiral Fokin are said to have given before sailing (“if they hole your hull,” “if they slap your face”) also vary from one account to another and are not confirmed in writing. In Arkhipov’s seat, what matters is not consent or refusal but whether to call the commander back on the bridge and make him read the situation again.

background.q: Why did the Americans not know about the tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba?
a: Besides the warheads for the medium-range missiles, there were tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba. On top of the two regiments of FKR cruise missiles in the memorandum of 24 May, Khrushchev added on 7–8 September an Il-28 detachment (six nuclear bombs) and three battalions of Luna (FROG) rockets (12 special warheads). The withdrawal order of 20 November lists six nuclear bombs, 12 Luna warheads and 80 FKR warheads. The number of nuclear warheads that reached Cuba varies by source: one annotated edition lists 24 R-14 warheads and 44 cruise missile warheads aboard the Aleksandrovsk, while General Garbuz testified to 183, strategic and tactical combined.

Whether the commander on the spot could use tactical nuclear weapons on his own authority is disputed. A draft directive to Pliyev of 8 September contains a passage allowing him, if the enemy landed and contact with Moscow was cut, to use the nuclear weapons of the Luna, Il-28 and FKR units on his own decision; but the draft is handwritten, and Malinovsky never signed it. The combat readiness order of the night of 22 October expressly excluded nuclear means, and cable No. 76639 of 27 October “categorically confirmed” the ban on any nuclear use without orders from Moscow. At the 1992 Havana conference General Gribkov claimed that authority had been delegated, but the majority view is that no delegation valid on paper ever existed.

US intelligence confirmed the R-12 sites, the Il-28 bombers and the Luna launchers from photographs, but did not know whether nuclear warheads lay beside them. When McNamara proposed on 16 October adding nuclear storage sites to the air strike targets, that too rested on guesswork. On 22 November Mikoyan told Castro that “the Americans do not even have information that tactical nuclear weapons are in Cuba.”

The tactical weapons were ordered out on 20 November, the day Khrushchev informed Kennedy that “all nuclear weapons have been taken out of Cuba,” and they left aboard the Atkarsk on 1 December. Until early November Moscow had meant to leave the Luna and FKR warheads in Cuba; Savranskaya reads the change of course as a response to the news that Castro had instructed his UN representative to insist Cuba must keep tactical nuclear weapons. Mikoyan cited a Soviet “law” forbidding the transfer of nuclear weapons to another country; no such law existed. The American participants first learned of the tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba at the 1992 Havana conference.
